questions.p:
Match each localized therapy with its role in hematological malignancies, according to the notes.
Therapy 1: surgery
Therapy 2: radiotherapy
Which pairing is correct, in order?
o: Curative in limited stage lymphoma, diagnosis only
CNS prophylaxis in ALL, palliation of AML
Diagnosis only, curative in limited stage lymphoma
Curative splenectomy, CNS prophylaxis in AML
questions.e:
Correct: C. Surgery is used for diagnosis only, such as resecting a lymph node. Radiotherapy can be curative in limited stage lymphoma and gives CNS prophylaxis in ALL.
A: This swaps the two roles.
B: Surgery is for diagnosis only, and the notes do not list radiation for AML palliation.
D: The notes do not list curative surgery, and CNS prophylaxis is listed for ALL.
Takeaway: In blood cancers, surgery mostly diagnoses. Radiation can cure limited disease.

questions.p: Which statement about mutations in myeloproliferative neoplasms is FALSE?
o: JAK2 mutations are found in 90 to 95% of PV
CALR mutations can drive essential thrombosis (ET)
MPL W515L/K mutations can drive primary myelofibrosis
JAK2 mutations are found in only 50 to 60% of PV
questions.e:
Correct: D. JAK2 is found in 90 to 95% of PV. The 50 to 60% figure belongs to ET and PMF.
A: This is true. JAK2 is found in 90 to 95% of PV.
B: This is true. CALR is listed for ET.
C: This is true. MPL W515L/K is listed for PMF.
Takeaway: JAK2: about 95% of PV, about half of ET and PMF. CALR and MPL cover much of the rest.

questions.p: A team planning a trial expects the new drug can only improve, never worsen, the response. Which choice lets them use a smaller sample size?
o: Adding a composite endpoint with unequal weights
questions.e:
Correct: B. A one-sided test is used when investigators suspect a difference in one direction only, and it needs a smaller sample size.
A: Power is 1 minus β, the chance of detecting a true difference. Cutting it defeats the trial's purpose.
C: A two-sided test is used when the direction is unknown.
D: Components of a composite endpoint are equally weighted.
Takeaway: One direction, smaller sample. Power = 1 minus β.

questions.p:
Which toxicities are common to all classic chemotherapies?
i) Myelosuppression
ii) Alopecia
iii) Mucositis
iv) Atrial fibrillation
questions.e:
Correct: A. The notes list myelosuppression, alopecia and mucositis as common to all classic chemotherapies.
B: Atrial fibrillation is an ibrutinib toxicity, and myelosuppression is missing.
C: Atrial fibrillation is an ibrutinib toxicity, and mucositis is missing.
D: Atrial fibrillation does not belong in the list.
Takeaway: Classic chemotherapy hits fast-dividing cells: marrow, hair, mucosa.

questions.p: Which statement about intention-to-treat (ITT) and per-protocol (PP) analysis is correct?
o: ITT includes only patients who finished treatment
ITT gives a more conservative effect estimate
PP analyzes everyone randomized, even dropouts
PP usually gives a lower effect estimate than ITT
questions.e:
Correct: B. ITT analyzes patients by assigned group, including those who stop treatment. It almost always gives a more conservative estimate and reflects real-world use.
A: Completers only is the definition of PP.
C: Analyzing everyone randomized is ITT, not PP.
D: PP usually yields a higher estimate, because patients doing poorly tend to drop out.
Takeaway: ITT is conservative and real world. PP inflates the effect.

questions.p: Investigators test a new oral drug for CLL that is less toxic and easier to take than standard therapy. They do not expect it to work better, only not meaningfully worse. Which trial design fits?
o: Phase 1, to find the tolerated dose
Equivalence, with no margin at all
questions.e:
Correct: C. A non-inferiority trial shows a new therapy is not clinically worse than the comparator. It suits a drug that offers other advantages such as safety, tolerability or convenience. The margin must be pre-specified.
A: A superiority trial aims to show the new therapy is better.
B: Phase 1 trials study safety and tolerated dose in 10 to 30 patients.
D: Equivalence trials still use lower and upper margins, and they test that two treatments differ by an unimportant amount.
Takeaway: Non-inferiority: give up a little efficacy (the delta) for safety or convenience.

questions.p:
Two patients have polycythemia vera.
Patient 1: 42, no history of thrombosis
Patient 2: 50, a DVT last year
Both take ASA 81 mg daily with a hematocrit target below 0.45. Which added therapy is correct for each, in order?
questions.e:
Correct: A. Low-risk PV is treated with phlebotomy. High risk means age 60 or older, or prior thrombosis, and adds cytoreduction with hydroxyurea with or without phlebotomy. Patient 2 is high risk because of the prior DVT.
B: Ruxolitinib and transplant are listed for primary myelofibrosis.
C: This reverses the risk groups.
D: Patient 2's prior thrombosis makes him high risk, which adds hydroxyurea.
Takeaway: High-risk PV: age 60 or older, or any prior thrombosis.

questions.p: Which statement about flow cytometry of a marrow aspirate is correct?
o: Samples must be formalin fixed before they are run
It detects changes in chromosome structure and number
FSC reflects granularity and SSC reflects cell size
FSC reflects cell size and SSC reflects granularity
questions.e:
Correct: D. In flow cytometry, forward scatter (FSC) measures size and side scatter (SSC) measures complexity or granularity.
A: Samples should be fresh (under 24 hours) and in liquid or disaggregated suspension.
B: Chromosome changes are studied by cytogenetics.
C: This reverses the two measures.
Takeaway: FSC is size, SSC is granularity. Immunophenotype is the pattern of antigens.

questions.p: Which plan fits CLL that is Rai stage 0 and causing no symptoms?
o: Refer for allogeneic stem cell transplant
questions.e:
Correct: D. Rai stage 0 is low risk. The notes say do NOT treat low risk or asymptomatic CLL.
A: Transplant is not a first step in asymptomatic, low-risk CLL.
B: Imatinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor for CML.
C: Chlorambucil is a CLL chemotherapy option once treatment is needed, not for stage 0 without symptoms.
Takeaway: CLL is incurable. Low-risk, asymptomatic CLL is watched, not treated.

questions.p: Which treatment do the notes list as curative in primary myelofibrosis?
o: Supportive red cell and platelet transfusions
questions.e:
Correct: A. The notes list allogeneic stem cell transplantation as the curative option for PMF.
B: Hydroxyurea is a conventional option for symptoms and quality of life.
C: Transfusions are supportive, not curative.
D: Ruxolitinib, a JAK inhibitor, is the newer option for symptom control.
Takeaway: PMF: transplant to cure, everything else to control symptoms.

questions.p:
Omar, 45, was diagnosed with AML this morning. Over a few hours he has become short of breath, with a headache, blurred vision and confusion. His oxygen saturation is 86% on room air. He has no fever.

Hb 82 g/L (ref 135-170)
WBC 210 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Blasts most of the white cells
Platelets 34 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
Potassium normal
Calcium normal

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: B. A very high blast count with dyspnea, hypoxia, headache, visual changes and confusion fits leukostasis. Big, sticky blasts get stuck in small vessels and reduce tissue perfusion.
A: Febrile neutropenia needs a fever.
C: TLS brings high potassium and phosphate, low calcium and kidney failure.
D: DIC presents with bleeding and abnormal clotting tests.
Takeaway: Leukostasis: IV fluids, leukapheresis and cytoreduction.

questions.p: A patient with CLL receives chlorambucil. Which mechanism matches this drug's class?
o: Interferes with cellular nucleic acid metabolism
Targets the CD20 marker on malignant B cells
Crosslinks guanine so DNA cannot enter S phase
Binds PD1 or PDL1 to release the immune brake
questions.e:
Correct: C. Chlorambucil is an alkylating agent. Alkylating agents crosslink guanine, causing cell arrest and apoptosis.
A: This is the antimetabolite mechanism, such as methotrexate.
B: CD20 targeting describes rituximab, a monoclonal antibody.
D: This is the immune checkpoint inhibitor mechanism.
Takeaway: Alkylators (cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, cisplatin, carboplatin) crosslink guanine.

questions.p:
Frank, 62, has smoked 2 packs a day for 40 years and has COPD on home oxygen at night. He has headaches in the morning. He has no itching after showers and no burning in his hands or feet. On exam he is plethoric with no enlarged spleen.

Hb 182 g/L (ref 135-170)
Hematocrit 0.55
WBC 8.1 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 260 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
Serum EPO high
JAK2 V617F negative

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. An isolated high Hb with a high EPO, negative JAK2 and a clear hypoxic cause in COPD and smoking fits secondary erythrocytosis. Treat the underlying cause.
A: CML gives a very high WBC with basophilia.
B: ET mainly raises platelets.
C: A tumour is possible with a high EPO, but his lung disease already explains it.
D: PV has a low EPO, usually a JAK2 mutation, and often a high WBC and platelets.
Takeaway: Primary means low EPO. Secondary means normal or high EPO.

questions.p: Why does the JAK2V617F mutation cause red cells to proliferate in polycythemia vera?
o: The mutant receptor signals without EPO
A tumour secretes EPO that drives the marrow
A congenital EPOR mutation lowers the threshold
The mutant receptor needs more EPO than normal
questions.e:
Correct: A. JAK2V617F is an acquired somatic mutation in the negative regulatory JH2 pseudokinase domain. The receptor is always phosphorylated and on, so it signals the STAT, PI3K and RAS-MAPK pathways without EPO.
B: Tumour EPO production is a secondary cause with normal or high EPO.
C: EPOR mutations are a rare congenital primary cause, while JAK2V617F is acquired.
D: This reverses the effect. The mutant does not require EPO at all.
Takeaway: JAK2V617F: valine to phenylalanine, acquired, constitutively on.

questions.p: Which statement about the epidemiology of the four leukemias is FALSE?
o: AML makes up 80% of acute adult leukemias
ALL makes up 80% of childhood leukemias
CML makes up 80% of childhood leukemias
CLL is the most common leukemia overall
questions.e:
Correct: C. CML accounts for only 5% of childhood leukemias. ALL makes up 80%.
A: This is true. AML is 80% of acute adult leukemias.
B: This is true. ALL is 80% of childhood leukemias.
D: This is true. CLL is 30% of all leukemias, the most common.
Takeaway: Children get ALL. Older adults get CLL. Adults with acute leukemia mostly have AML.

questions.p:
Match each patient with the targeted therapy the notes list for their disease.
Patient 1: multiple myeloma
Patient 2: acute promyelocytic leukemia
Patient 3: chronic lymphocytic leukemia
Which pairing is correct, in order?
questions.e:
Correct: B. The notes list bortezomib (proteasome inhibitor) for MM, all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) for APL, and ibrutinib (Bruton kinase inhibitor) for CLL.
A: Ibrutinib is for CLL, and bortezomib is for MM.
C: Imatinib treats CML, and ATRA is not a CLL drug.
D: ATRA treats APL, not myeloma.
Takeaway: Targeted therapy pairs: CML imatinib, APL ATRA, CLL ibrutinib, MM bortezomib.

questions.p: Which therapy is the long-term mainstay for chronic phase CML?
questions.e:
Correct: D. The notes list tyrosine kinase inhibitors (imatinib, nilotinib, dasatinib) as the chronic treatment for CML, with prophylactic allopurinol.
A: Chlorambucil and fludarabine are CLL chemotherapies.
B: ATRA treats APL.
C: 7+3 is AML induction.
Takeaway: CML: a TKI for the long term, transplant as a possible cure.

questions.p:
Nadia, 19, has 1 week of fever, a very sore throat, fatigue and tender swollen neck nodes. Her roommate had the same illness last month. On exam she has large tonsils with exudate and a tender spleen tip.

Hb 132 g/L (ref 115-160)
WBC 13.8 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Lymphocytes high
Platelets 172 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
Film: atypical lymphocytes surrounding the red cells. No smudge cells, no blasts.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. A young adult with fever, sore throat, tender nodes, a tender spleen and atypical lymphocytes surrounding red cells has EBV mononucleosis.
A: ALL shows blasts.
B: CLL affects older adults and shows smudge cells.
C: Hodgkin lymphoma doesn't cause atypical lymphocytes in the blood.
D: Her lymphocytes are high, not her neutrophils.
Takeaway: Confirm with a Monospot test. Do flow cytometry only if it persists past 4 to 6 weeks.

questions.p:
Ava, 19, started induction chemotherapy for ALL 2 days ago. She now has palpitations, muscle cramps and very little urine output. Her ECG shows peaked T waves. She has no fever, bleeding or confusion.

Hb 88 g/L (ref 115-160)
WBC 2.1 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 61 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
Potassium high
Phosphate high
Uric acid high
Calcium low
Creatinine rising

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: C. Starting treatment for a leukemia, then high potassium, phosphate and urate, low calcium, a rising creatinine and arrhythmia risk fit tumour lysis syndrome. Dying tumour cells release their contents into the blood.
A: Febrile neutropenia needs a fever.
B: Leukostasis brings dyspnea, hypoxia and confusion with a very high blast count.
D: DIC presents with bleeding.
Takeaway: Prevent and treat with hydration and allopurinol or rasburicase.

questions.p:
Which of the following are part of the management of leukostasis?
i) IV fluids
ii) Leukapheresis
iii) Cytoreduction
iv) Rasburicase
questions.e:
Correct: A. The notes list IV fluids, leukapheresis and cytoreduction for leukostasis.
B: Rasburicase belongs to tumour lysis syndrome, and IV fluids are missing.
C: Rasburicase belongs to tumour lysis syndrome, and leukapheresis is missing.
D: Rasburicase is not part of the leukostasis plan.
Takeaway: Leukostasis: fluids, leukapheresis, cytoreduction. TLS: hydration, rasburicase, allopurinol, dialysis.

questions.p:
Leo, 4, has 3 weeks of pallor, bruising, limping from leg pain and two fevers. On exam he has neck nodes, a large liver and spleen, and petechiae. Chest X-ray shows a mediastinal mass.

Hb 68 g/L (ref 110-140)
WBC 36 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 22 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
LDH high
Film: many blasts with no granules.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. A young child with marrow failure, bone pain, nodes, organ enlargement, a mediastinal mass and agranular blasts has ALL, 80% of childhood leukemias.
A: ITP lowers platelets only.
B: Mono shows atypical lymphocytes, not blasts.
C: AML blasts often carry an Auer rod, and AML is 15% of childhood leukemias.
D: Aplastic anemia shows no blasts or organ enlargement.
Takeaway: Before chemotherapy, do a lumbar puncture to check for CNS involvement.

questions.p: A patient on pembrolizumab develops diarrhea and is diagnosed with colitis. What is the best treatment for this toxicity?
questions.e:
Correct: B. Pembrolizumab is an immune checkpoint inhibitor. It takes the brakes off the immune system, which causes immune toxicities such as colitis, pneumonitis, rash and hepatitis. These are treated with glucocorticoids.
A: Vancomycin is added in febrile neutropenia with skin or line infection.
C: Rasburicase treats tumour lysis syndrome.
D: Leukapheresis treats leukostasis.
Takeaway: Checkpoint inhibitor toxicity is immune-mediated, so treat with steroids.

questions.p: Four neutropenic patients on chemotherapy report fevers. Which one meets the definition of febrile neutropenia?
questions.e:
Correct: D. Febrile neutropenia is a single oral temperature above 38.3°C, or 38.0°C or higher sustained over 1 hour.
A: A single reading of 38.1°C is below the 38.3°C single-reading cutoff.
B: 37.9°C never reaches 38.0°C, however long it lasts.
C: A single 38.2°C reading is still below 38.3°C.
Takeaway: Two ways in: one reading above 38.3°C, or 38.0°C or more for over an hour.

questions.p: Daniel, 34, has schizophrenia and started clozapine three months ago. His ANC is 0.8 × 10^9/L. He has no fever. Which description fits best?
o: Moderate neutropenia from a congenital cause
Mild neutropenia from an autoimmune cause
questions.e:
Correct: A. An ANC of 0.5 to 0.99 × 10^9/L is moderate neutropenia. Clozapine is a listed acquired toxin cause.
B: A new drug and adult onset point to an acquired cause, not a congenital one.
C: Severe neutropenia is below 0.5 × 10^9/L.
D: Mild is 1 to 1.5 × 10^9/L, and nothing here suggests autoimmunity.
Takeaway: ANC bands: mild 1 to 1.5, moderate 0.5 to 0.99, severe below 0.5.

questions.p:
Two patients have APL.
Patient 1: WBC 2.1 × 10^9/L, abundant cytoplasmic granules
Patient 2: WBC 24 × 10^9/L, few granules
Which subtypes fit, in order?
questions.e:
Correct: B. The hypergranular or typical form (M3, 75% of cases) usually has a decreased WBC. The microgranular form (M3v, 25%) has a WBC above 10.
A: This reverses the two subtypes.
C: A high WBC with few granules fits M3v.
D: M4 and M5 are monoblastic and monocytic leukemias, not APL.
Takeaway: APL: M3 has a low WBC and many granules. M3v has a high WBC and few granules.

questions.p: A patient with ALL receives vincristine. How does it stop tumour cells from dividing?
o: Binds stabilized microtubules so chromosomes cannot be pulled apart
Interferes with normal nucleic acid metabolism
Crosslinks guanine so DNA cannot enter S phase
questions.e:
Correct: C. Vincristine is a vinca alkaloid. Vinca alkaloids inhibit microtubule assembly in metaphase and disrupt M phase.
A: Binding stabilized microtubules is the taxane mechanism (paclitaxel, docetaxel).
B: Disrupted nucleic acid metabolism is the antimetabolite mechanism.
D: Guanine crosslinking is the alkylating agent mechanism.
Takeaway: Both vincas and taxanes block M phase, by opposite actions on microtubules.

questions.p: In the initial assessment of a patient with febrile neutropenia, which action should be avoided?
questions.e:
Correct: D. The notes specify the GI exam in febrile neutropenia is done with no DRE.
A: Blood and urine cultures are part of the initial investigations.
B: A chest x-ray is part of the initial investigations.
C: Skin and indwelling IV catheter sites are part of the focused exam.
Takeaway: Examine mouth, sinuses, lungs, abdomen, GU, skin and lines, but skip the DRE.

questions.p:
Match each finding with a benign cause the notes list.
Patient 1: eosinophilia after starting penicillin
Patient 2: basophilia with fatigue and cold intolerance
Patient 3: monocytosis with a chronic cough and night sweats
Which pairing is correct, in order?
questions.e:
Correct: B. Eosinophilia lists drug reaction (penicillin). Basophilia lists hypothyroidism. Monocytosis lists chronic infection (TB).
A: Parasites cause eosinophilia, but the penicillin history points to a drug reaction, and the other two pairings are wrong.
C: Hypothyroidism causes basophilia, not eosinophilia.
D: TB causes monocytosis, and hypothyroidism causes basophilia.
Takeaway: Eosinophils: drugs, allergy, parasites. Basophils: hypothyroidism. Monocytes: TB, endocarditis, IBD.

questions.p: After remission in childhood ALL, which describes the maintenance phase?
o: No further treatment unless symptoms return
Treatment ends after a 4 to 6 month course of chemotherapy
Low-dose intermittent chemotherapy for 2 to 3 years
A tyrosine kinase inhibitor taken indefinitely
questions.e:
Correct: C. ALL follows the Dana-Farber protocol over 2 to 3 years. Maintenance gives low-dose intermittent chemotherapy over 2 to 3 years to prevent relapse.
A: Watch and wait applies to low-risk, asymptomatic CLL.
B: A 4 to 6 month course with 4 to 6 weeks in hospital is the AML timeline.
D: Chronic tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy is the CML approach.
Takeaway: ALL treatment runs 2 to 3 years: induction, consolidation, then maintenance, plus CNS and testes prophylaxis.

questions.p: A patient has relapsed ALL and is referred for tisagenlecleucel (Kymriah). Which description fits this therapy?
o: Modified T cells made from the patient's own blood
An antibody linking a tumour marker to a T cell
An antibody that carries a radioisotope to CD markers
A naked monoclonal antibody that targets CD20
questions.e:
Correct: A. Tisagenlecleucel is a CAR-T cell therapy, listed for ALL and relapsed DLBCL. CAR-T cells are genetically modified T cells from the patient's own blood.
B: Linking a tumour marker to a cytotoxic T cell describes a bi-specific antibody.
C: A radioisotope-carrying antibody is a conjugated antibody, such as Zevalin.
D: A naked CD20 antibody is rituximab.
Takeaway: CAR-T: the patient's own T cells, modified to attack the cancer.

questions.p: In a trial, 20% of the control group and 15% of the treatment group have a relapse. Which set of results is correct?
questions.e:
Correct: D. ARR = 20% minus 15% = 5%. RR = 15 ÷ 20 = 0.75, so RRR = 1 minus 0.75 = 25%. NNT is the number treated to prevent one bad outcome, 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20.
A: 75% is the relative risk, not the relative risk reduction.
B: This swaps ARR and RRR.
C: 15% is the treatment group's risk, not the ARR.
Takeaway: ARR is a subtraction. RRR = 1 minus RR. NNT = 1 ÷ ARR.

questions.p:
Mei, 58, has 2 weeks of fatigue, fevers, easy bruising and pain over her breastbone. She has gum swelling and a few purple skin nodules. On exam she has petechiae, gum infiltration and sternal tenderness.

Hb 76 g/L (ref 115-160)
WBC 54 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 24 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
LDH high
Uric acid high
Film: many large blast cells, one with an Auer rod.
Flow cytometry: myeloid blasts.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. Marrow failure, sternal tenderness, gum and skin infiltration, and large myeloid blasts with an Auer rod fit AML, 80% of acute leukemias in adults.
A: ALL blasts have no granules or Auer rods.
B: CLL shows mature lymphocytes and smudge cells.
C: MDS doesn't have this many blasts.
D: CML shows mature myeloid cells with basophilia.
Takeaway: AML induction is 7+3 chemotherapy.

questions.p:
Ruth, 58, has episodes of burning, red toes and has had two brief spells of blurred vision. She has no heavy periods, recent surgery, infection, inflammatory disease or cancer. On exam she has no enlarged spleen.

Hb 134 g/L (ref 115-160)
WBC 8.0 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 720 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
Ferritin normal
CRP normal
CALR positive
Marrow: increased enlarged, mature megakaryocytes with hyperlobulated nuclei.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. A platelet count of 450 or more with erythromelalgia and ocular migraines, a CALR mutation, big hyperlobulated megakaryocytes and no reactive cause fits essential thrombocythemia.
A: Myelofibrosis shows teardrop cells and marrow fibrosis.
B: CML gives a high WBC with basophilia.
C: Her iron, CRP and history rule out a reactive cause.
D: PV needs a high Hb.
Takeaway: ET carries a risk of both thrombosis and bleeding.

questions.p: A 70-year-old's marrow core biopsy shows 70% cellularity. The myeloid to erythroid ratio is 2:1. How should you interpret the biopsy?
o: Normal cellularity for age, normal M:E ratio
Hypocellular for age, high M:E ratio
Hypercellular for age, normal M:E ratio
questions.e:
Correct: D. Expected cellularity is 100 minus age, so 30% for a 70-year-old. 70% is hypercellular. A ratio of 2:1 sits within the normal 1:1 to 3:1 range.
A: 70% is far above the expected 30%.
B: 70% is not low for a 70-year-old, and 2:1 is normal.
C: The marrow is more cellular than expected, and 2:1 is normal.
Takeaway: Marrow cellularity = 100 minus age. Normal M:E ratio is 1:1 to 3:1.

questions.p:
Which of the following cause pancytopenia through decreased production?
i) Aplastic anemia
ii) Myelofibrosis
iii) Vitamin deficiencies
iv) Splenomegaly
questions.e:
Correct: C. Aplastic anemia, myelofibrosis and vitamin deficiencies are listed under decreased production.
A: Splenomegaly causes sequestration, and aplastic anemia is missing.
B: Splenomegaly causes pancytopenia by sequestration, not decreased production.
D: Splenomegaly belongs to sequestration.
Takeaway: Pancytopenia: decreased production, increased destruction, or sequestration.

questions.p:
Isabel, 38, has 5 days of gum bleeding, heavy bruising and a nosebleed that won't stop. Today she has a sudden headache. On exam she has petechiae, oozing gums and no enlarged nodes or spleen.

Hb 84 g/L (ref 115-160)
WBC 1.9 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 19 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
PT/INR 1.9
Fibrinogen 0.8 g/L
D-dimer high
Film: abnormal promyelocytes, several with multiple Auer rods in one cell.
Flow cytometry: HLA-DR negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. Pancytopenia with DIC, blasts with 2 or more Auer rods and HLA-DR negative flow fit APL. Its main early danger is fatal bleeding, often in the brain.
A: ITP has normal clotting tests and no abnormal cells.
B: CML gives a high WBC with basophilia.
C: Aplastic anemia has no abnormal cells or DIC.
D: ALL blasts have no granules or Auer rods.
Takeaway: Confirm with t(15;17) or PML/RARα, and start ATRA.

questions.p:
George, 70, has 6 months of fatigue, early satiety, night sweats and weight loss. On exam his spleen reaches his pelvis. He has no enlarged nodes.

Hb 88 g/L (ref 135-170)
WBC 3.1 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Platelets 84 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
LDH high
JAK2 V617F positive
Film: teardrop cells, nucleated red cells and immature myeloid cells.
Marrow core biopsy: marrow fibrosis.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. Pancytopenia from marrow fibrosis, a massive spleen, teardrop cells with a leukoerythroblastic picture and a JAK2 mutation fit primary myelofibrosis.
A: CML gives a high WBC with basophilia.
B: Myelophthisis also shows teardrop cells, but he has no cancer history, and the JAK2 mutation points to an MPN.
C: MDS shows dysplasia, not marrow fibrosis with a massive spleen.
D: Aplastic anemia shows a fatty, empty marrow and no large spleen.
Takeaway: Allogeneic stem cell transplant is the only cure.

questions.p:
Harold, 74, has a CBC at his annual physical. He feels well, with no fever, weight loss or night sweats. On exam he has small, painless nodes in both armpits and no enlarged liver or spleen.

Hb 138 g/L (ref 135-170)
WBC 32 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Lymphocytes 28, mature-looking × 10⁹/L
Platelets 205 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
Film: many small mature lymphocytes and smudge cells.
Flow cytometry: clonal B cells that are CD5, CD19, dim CD20 and CD23 positive.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: B. An older man with a high count of mature lymphocytes, smudge cells and clonal B cells with the CD5, CD19, dim CD20 and CD23 pattern has CLL, the most common leukemia.
A: Mononucleosis shows atypical lymphocytes in a young person and is not clonal.
C: A reactive lymphocytosis is not clonal.
D: CML raises myeloid cells with basophilia.
E: ALL shows blasts.
Takeaway: Don't treat low-risk, asymptomatic CLL.

questions.p:
Sofia, 30, has 4 days of fever, cough with green sputum and pain on breathing in. Chest X-ray shows a left lower lobe consolidation. She has no weight loss, night sweats or enlarged spleen.

Hb 128 g/L (ref 115-160)
WBC 18 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Neutrophils 15, with bands × 10⁹/L
Basophils normal
Eosinophils normal
Platelets 390 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
Film: toxic granules, toxic vacuoles and Döhle bodies. No myeloblasts or promyelocytes.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: A. Mature neutrophils with a left shift, toxic changes, no blasts or promyelocytes, and an obvious pneumonia fit a secondary, reactive neutrophilia.
B: AML shows blasts.
C: Leukostasis needs a very high blast count.
D: Primary neutrophilia shows immature myeloid cells, often with a WBC over 30.
E: CML shows basophilia, eosinophilia and myelocytes, often with a large spleen.
Takeaway: Primary neutrophilia: immature cells and often a WBC over 30.

questions.p:
Rajiv, 68, has 2 months of night sweats, weight loss and a dragging feeling under his left ribs. He has no fevers or infections. On exam his spleen is palpable 8 cm below the costal margin. He has no lymph nodes.

Hb 118 g/L (ref 135-170)
WBC 148 × 10⁹/L (ref 4-10)
Basophils increased
Eosinophils increased
Platelets 610 × 10⁹/L (ref 150-450)
Film: a bimodal spread of myelocytes and neutrophils, few blasts.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e:
Correct: E. A very high WBC with basophilia, eosinophilia, thrombocytosis and a bimodal spread of myelocytes and neutrophils, plus a large spleen, fits chronic phase CML.
A: Myelofibrosis gives cytopenias and teardrop cells.
B: CLL raises mature lymphocytes, with smudge cells.
C: A reactive neutrophilia has no basophilia and shows toxic granules, with a clear trigger.
D: AML shows many large blasts.
Takeaway: Confirm with FISH for t(9;22) BCR-ABL.
